newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece says Turk troops must quit Cyprus for talks.
newsitem.headline: Greece says Turk troops must quit Cyprus for talks.

text.p: Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis called on Turkey on Tuesday to withdraw its troops from northern Cyprus to help make pending U.N.-sponsored talks on reuniting the Mediterranean island successful.
"The Turkish occupation must end. This is the only way to find a solution to the Cyprus problem," Simitis told reporters after talks with Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides.

Clerides will meet Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash next week for the first time in three years in yet another effort to end the island's division that dates to 1974 when Turkey invaded and occupied the northern third with about 30,000 troops.
"We are going to the negotiations with goodwill but are determined to safeguard our rights. Athens and Nicosia (Greek Cypriot government) have a common line, " Clerides said.
Clerides and Denktash will meet July 9-13 at a rural retreat called Troutbeck 145 km (90 miles) north of New York City after an invitation by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan.
The U.N. Security Council has welcomed Annan's decision to launch a "sustained process of direct negotiations between the leaders of the two Cypriot communities."

Turkey's invasion of Cyprus was triggered by a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece. Turkish Cypriots proclaimed their own state in the north of Cyprus in 1983 with Denktash as president, but their entity is recognised only by the government of Turkey.
The United Nations, which has had peacekeepers patrolling a tense "Green Line" dividing Cyprus since the mid-1970s, has been trying for years to reunite the island under a federal system.

The Security Council resolution called on Cypriot leaders to "commit themselves to this process of negotiations and ... cooperate actively and constructively with the secretary-general and his special adviser on Cyprus."
"The positions of the two sides have not changed," a senior Greek government official told Reuters. "There is no guarantee that there will be progress during this latest round of talks."
U.S. President Bill Clinton has appointed former Bosnia peace negotiator Richard Holbrooke to help resolve the Cyprus problem but Holbrooke has said he does expect a swift breakthrough.

The Greek Cypriot government is scheduled to start talks for accession to the European Union in the first half of 1998 but Greece's EU partners have expressed reservations whether this is possible with the island divided.
Nicosia announced plans earlier this year to buy Russian-made S-300 air defence missiles, scheduled for delivery in 1998. Ankara has threatened to use force if the missiles are deployed.
But Clerides said the deployment would go ahead as scheduled.
Greece and Turkey, although nominally allies within NATO, have often come close to war over the Cyprus problem and mineral and territorial rights in the Aegean Sea.
